nodes.label: The Seleucid Empire
nodes.full: The Hellenistic successor state ruling Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran after Alexander — the power that administers Tylos, garrisons it, brings Greek as its language of government, and whose kings (Antiochus III) campaign in the Gulf.
nodes.src: background; the Seleucid Gulf (Potts 1990, vol.2)

nodes.label: Palmyra — the Syrian desert caravan city
nodes.full: Palmyra, the oasis city linking the Syrian desert to Mesopotamia, sends merchants and caravan leaders to Spasinou Charax and supplies men who serve as 'satrap of Tylos' for the Characene king.
nodes.src: background — see the palmyrene-100bc-273ce folio

nodes.label: Seleucid administration of Tylos and the Erythraean islands
nodes.full: After Alexander, Bahrain became 'Tylos', an island under Seleucid oversight. A Greek inscription names a 'governor of Tylos and Dilmun', and the towns took Greek forms — the Gulf's brief Hellenistic moment.
nodes.src: Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi (2002); Strabo 16.3.4

nodes.label: The Abiel coinage — rulers of the lower Gulf
nodes.full: Silver coins struck at Mleiha copy Alexander tetradrachms but carry the Aramaic name 'Abiel', sometimes 'Abiel daughter of...' — the name of a ruler or dynasty of the Oman peninsula kingdom the Greeks called Omana.
nodes.src: Potts, "The Pre-Islamic Coinage of Eastern Arabia" (1991, 2002)

nodes.label: Mleiha — fort, palace and royal necropolis
nodes.full: Mleiha was the inland capital: a mud-brick fort with corner towers, a large columned building, a mint, iron workshops and a cemetery of monumental tower-tombs with camel and horse burials. It is the seat of the Abiel power.
nodes.src: Mouton, "La péninsule d'Oman de la fin de l'âge du Fer..." (2008)

nodes.label: Characene draws Tylos into its orbit
nodes.full: Hyspaosines founded the kingdom of Characene at the head of the Gulf, and its kings came to dominate Tylos and the sea lanes. Characene coins circulate throughout the Gulf; a Characene satrap of Tylos is attested.
nodes.src: Characene coinage; Pliny NH 6.147; Isidore of Charax

nodes.label: Ardashir I ends the Parthian Gulf order
nodes.full: al-Tabari records that Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian Empire, campaigned in eastern Arabia and killed the king of Bahrain, named as Sanatruq. Mleiha was abandoned within a generation; the Gulf passed under Sasanian control.
nodes.src: al-Tabari I.820 (Bosworth trans.); Mouton (2008)

nodes.label: Antiochus III's expedition against Gerrha
nodes.full: Returning from the east, Antiochus III sailed against the caravan city of Gerrha. Its people met him with an embassy and a vast payment — 500 talents of silver, a thousand talents of frankincense — and he sailed away, leaving them their independence.
nodes.src: Polybius 13.9

nodes.label: Contest for the head of the Gulf
nodes.full: Characene's control of the Gulf's most valuable choke-point made it a recurring target for the Parthian kings and, briefly, for Trajan's Rome (116 AD). The instability at the Gulf head shaped who could trade down its length.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio 68.28-29; Schuol, "Die Charakene" (2000)

nodes.label: The destruction and abandonment of Mleiha
nodes.full: Mleiha's fort shows a burning and rebuilding in the 2nd century, then final abandonment in the 3rd. The end of the Abiel kingdom coincides with the rise of the Sasanians and a shift of activity to the coast.
nodes.src: Mleiha fort stratigraphy (Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority)

nodes.label: Ardashir's Arabian campaign
nodes.full: Ardashir I's move into eastern Arabia — attested by al-Tabari — brought the whole Gulf under a single imperial power for the first time since the Achaemenids and closed the Parthian-era world of independent coin-kings.
nodes.src: al-Tabari I.820; Potts (1990) vol.2

nodes.label: A governor 'of Tylos and the islands'
nodes.full: A Greek dedication from Bahrain records an official responsible for Tylos and the neighbouring islands — evidence that the Seleucids ran the Gulf as a defined administrative district, with Greek as its language of government.
nodes.src: Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi, Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 13 (2002)

nodes.label: Local minting at Mleiha
nodes.full: The Oman peninsula kingdom struck its own silver — first close copies of Alexander types, then increasingly local designs and legends. Issuing coinage was a claim to sovereignty as much as a convenience for trade.
nodes.src: Potts (1991); die studies of the Mleiha mint

nodes.label: Hasaitic funerary inscriptions and their formulae
nodes.full: Dozens of tombstones in the eastern Arabian 'Hasaitic' script name the deceased, their lineage and a protective deity, sometimes with a curse on anyone who disturbs the grave — the region's own legal-religious response to the Hellenistic epigraphic habit.
nodes.src: Sima, "Die hasaitischen Inschriften" (1999)

nodes.label: Characene coinage as a Gulf-wide currency
nodes.full: The tetradrachms and drachms of the Characene kings turn up in hoards and site finds the length of the Gulf. Whoever controlled Charax effectively set the coinage that Gulf merchants used.
nodes.src: Characene coins in Gulf hoards; Schuol, "Die Charakene" (2000)

nodes.label: The temple of Shams at ed-Dur
nodes.full: A small square temple at ed-Dur, with altars and a well, was dedicated to Shams, the sun deity, named in an Aramaic inscription on the site. It is the best-preserved pre-Islamic temple in the UAE.
nodes.src: Belgian mission at ed-Dur (Haerinck)

nodes.label: Greek cult on Tylos
nodes.full: Hellenistic Bahrain has yielded Greek votive inscriptions, including a dedication to the Dioscuri, and figurines in Greek style. Greek religion arrived with the garrison and the traders and coexisted with older Gulf cults.
nodes.src: Gatier, Lombard & Al-Sindi (2002); Hellenistic terracottas

nodes.label: Camel and horse burials at Mleiha and ed-Dur
nodes.full: Elite tombs at Mleiha were accompanied by the burials of camels, and sometimes horses, often with harness and saddlery. The rite ties the warrior aristocracy of the Abiel kingdom to their mounts in death.
nodes.src: Mleiha animal burials (Mouton; Jasim, "The Necropolis of Mleiha", 1999)

nodes.label: Aramaic and the goddess of the eastern Arabian tombs
nodes.full: Hasaitic tomb texts invoke a small pantheon — chiefly a goddess whose name is written 'at' — to protect the dead. Eastern Arabia kept its own religion while writing it in a script shaped by contact with the Aramaic and South Arabian worlds.
nodes.src: Sima (1999); the divine name and its possible link to Athtar / Allat

nodes.label: The tower tombs of Mleiha
nodes.full: Mleiha's dead of rank were buried under square mud-brick towers, some plastered and multi-storeyed, standing above ground as visible monuments. They revive, in a new form, the peninsula's old habit of monumental burial.
nodes.src: Jasim, "The Necropolis of Mleiha" (1999); Mouton (2008)

nodes.label: The Thaj gold funerary set
nodes.full: A child or young woman at Thaj was buried with a gold face-mask, a gold-mesh glove, pearl-and-gold earrings, a necklace of gold and rubies and a girdle. It is the richest pre-Islamic burial known from eastern Arabia.
nodes.src: The 'Thaj treasure', excavated 1998; 'Roads of Arabia'

nodes.label: Imported luxury at ed-Dur
nodes.full: ed-Dur produced Roman cast and mould-blown glass, a Roman bronze figurine, Rhodian and Mesopotamian amphorae, Parthian glazed jars and Indian pottery — a coastal town furnished from every shore of the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean.
nodes.src: ed-Dur excavation series; the ed-Dur glass corpus (Whitehouse)

nodes.label: The Abiel coins as portraiture
nodes.full: Over generations the Herakles head on the Mleiha coins drifts away from its Greek model into a distinctive local style — stylised curls, large eye, added symbols. The series is a small case study in an imported art form being made one's own.
nodes.src: Potts (1991), on the stylistic devolution of the Abiel series

nodes.label: Androsthenes of Thasos surveys the Gulf for Alexander
nodes.full: Alexander sent three captains to explore the Arabian shore; Androsthenes sailed furthest and wrote a lost 'Voyage along the Indian Coast' describing Tylos, its pearls and its 'wool-bearing trees'. It is the first scientific account of the Gulf.
nodes.src: Androsthenes cited by Theophrastus (HP 4.7) and Strabo (16.3)

nodes.label: Cotton on Tylos — Theophrastus's 'wool-bearing trees'
nodes.full: Theophrastus, drawing on Androsthenes, describes trees on Tylos that bear wool — cotton, grown and spun on Bahrain around 300 BC. It is among the earliest records of cotton cultivation west of India.
nodes.src: Theophrastus, "Historia Plantarum" 4.7.7-8

nodes.label: A trilingual epigraphic culture
nodes.full: Eastern Arabia in this period writes in Greek (Bahrain), Aramaic (ed-Dur, coins), and the local Hasaitic script (tombstones) — sometimes on the same sites. After a millennium of near-silence, the region is literate again, in several traditions at once.
nodes.src: Greek: Gatier et al. (2002); Aramaic: coin legends; Hasaitic: Sima (1999)

nodes.label: Gerrha, 'the richest of all tribes'
nodes.full: Strabo and Pliny describe Gerrha as fabulously wealthy on the incense trade: south Arabian frankincense and myrrh came overland to Gerrha and were shipped up the Gulf, or sent by caravan to Petra and the Mediterranean. Its people, they say, built with blocks of salt.
nodes.src: Strabo 16.3.3; Pliny NH 6.147-150; Agatharchides

nodes.label: Omana — the Gulf's port on the India run
nodes.full: The 'Periplus of the Erythraean Sea' names Omana as a Gulf port trading directly with the Indian coast — sending out pearls, purple, dates, wine and slaves, taking in copper, teak, sandalwood and ebony. ed-Dur is its likeliest site.
nodes.src: 'Periplus Maris Erythraei' §36 (Casson ed., 1989)

nodes.label: The pearls of Tylos
nodes.full: Greek and Roman writers single out Tylos for its pearls — Isidore of Charax, Pliny and others describe the fishery and the trade. The Gulf's oldest industry was now a name-brand luxury in the Roman Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Isidore of Charax; Pliny NH 9.106; Athenaeus 3.93

nodes.label: Mleiha, the Gulf's iron town
nodes.full: Mleiha held the largest concentration of iron-smelting furnaces yet found in south-east Arabia, turning out tools and weapons. The Abiel kingdom's wealth rested on manufacturing as well as on transit trade.
nodes.src: Mleiha metallurgical area (Mouton; Sharjah Archaeology Authority)

nodes.label: Characene and the Charax-India axis
nodes.full: Charax, at the mouth of the Tigris, was where goods from India and the Gulf met the caravan roads to Palmyra and the Parthian interior. Its kings grew rich as gatekeepers, and their coinage financed the whole Gulf trade.
nodes.src: Isidore of Charax; the Palmyrene trade inscriptions; Schuol (2000)

nodes.label: Iron smelting at scale
nodes.full: Batteries of small shaft furnaces at Mleiha, with their slag heaps and ore stores, represent the peninsula's first large iron industry — the technology that armed the Abiel aristocracy and equipped its trade.
nodes.src: Mleiha iron-working area, French mission reports

nodes.label: The mud-brick fort of Mleiha
nodes.full: A square enclosure with projecting corner towers and a central courtyard building, rebuilt after a burning — Mleiha's fort is the peninsula's first true fortification since the Bronze Age towers, adapted to a world of cavalry and iron weapons.
nodes.src: Mleiha fort excavation (Boucharlat; Mouton)

nodes.label: Monsoon sailing on the Gulf-India route
nodes.full: By the 1st century AD, Gulf shippers were using the seasonal monsoon winds to run directly to and from the Indian coast, as the Periplus describes for Omana. Larger sewn-plank vessels made the open-water crossing routine.
nodes.src: 'Periplus Maris Erythraei' on the sailing seasons; Casson (1989)

nodes.label: The Gulf as Rome's back door to India
nodes.full: When Red Sea routes were taxed or blocked, Indian goods flowed instead up the Gulf: from the Indian coast to Omana, on to Charax, and overland to Palmyra and the Mediterranean. The Gulf was the alternative artery of the Rome-India trade.
nodes.src: 'Periplus' §36; the Palmyrene caravan inscriptions; Young, "Rome's Eastern Trade" (2001)

nodes.label: Palmyrene merchants at Spasinou Charax
nodes.full: Palmyra's trade inscriptions repeatedly honour citizens who led caravans to Charax or served as 'satrap of Tylos' for the Characene king. A resident Palmyrene community linked the Syrian desert city to the Gulf.
nodes.src: Palmyrene tariff and honorific inscriptions; a Palmyrene as 'satrap of Tylos'

nodes.label: Roman and Parthian goods on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: Roman glass and bronzes, Parthian glazed pottery, Rhodian wine amphorae and Indian ceramics arrive together at ed-Dur. The lower Gulf coast consumed the products of every surrounding civilisation and re-exported many of them.
nodes.src: ed-Dur imports (Belgian and Danish missions); Haerinck, "Excavations at ed-Dur"

nodes.label: Indians and Characenes at ed-Dur
nodes.full: Indian cooking pots, a possible Brahmi graffito and quantities of Characene coin at ed-Dur suggest resident foreign traders — Indian and Mesopotamian — living in the port alongside its Arabian population.
nodes.src: Indian Red Polished Ware at ed-Dur; the site's coin profile (heavily Characene)

nodes.label: Gerrha's caravans to Petra and the Mediterranean
nodes.full: Overland caravans carried Gerrhaean goods across the peninsula to the Nabataean network and the ports of the Levant. Eastern Arabia's incense wealth and Nabataean Petra's were two ends of the same road.
nodes.src: Strabo 16.4.4 on the Gerrha-Nabataea caravan route

nodes.label: Alexander's Arabian project
nodes.full: Alexander planned to circumnavigate Arabia and settle colonies on Tylos and on Icarus (Failaka), sending survey ships ahead. His death in Babylon left the scheme unexecuted — but Greek names and settlers reached the Gulf anyway.
nodes.src: Arrian, "Anabasis" 7.19-20; the Failaka ('Ikaros') Greek sanctuary

nodes.label: Characene emerges as an independent Gulf kingdom
nodes.full: As Seleucid power collapsed, Hyspaosines carved out the kingdom of Characene at the Gulf head. For the next 350 years an independent, coin-minting state controlled the point where the Gulf trade met Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Characene foundation c.127 BC (Schuol 2000); Hyspaosines' coinage

nodes.label: Rome and Parthia fight over the trade roads
nodes.full: The long Roman-Parthian contest over Armenia and Mesopotamia repeatedly disrupted the overland routes, pushing traffic onto the Gulf and making Characene and Palmyra alternately rich and vulnerable.
nodes.src: Cassius Dio and Tacitus on the Roman-Parthian wars; Young (2001)

nodes.label: The Sasanians replace the Parthians
nodes.full: Ardashir I's overthrow of the Parthian Arsacids brought a centralising dynasty to Iran that took direct interest in the Gulf. Within two decades the age of independent Gulf coin-kings was over.
nodes.src: Battle of Hormozdgan (224 AD); Ardashir's Gulf campaigns (al-Tabari)

nodes.label: The gold-mask burial of Thaj
nodes.full: The richest pre-Islamic grave in eastern Arabia belongs to a girl or young woman, buried with a gold face-mask and a fortune in gold, pearls and rubies. Whatever her personal status, her family channelled enormous wealth into a female burial.
nodes.src: The Thaj treasure (Saudi excavations, 1998)

nodes.label: Women as tomb-owners in the Hasaitic texts
nodes.full: Hasaitic tombstones sometimes name a woman as the person for whom the tomb was made, and frequently trace descent through the mother. Eastern Arabian commemoration gave women a visible place in the record.
nodes.src: Sima (1999); the frequency of matronymics in the corpus

nodes.label: Was Abiel a queen?
nodes.full: Some Mleiha coins read 'Abiel daughter of...', a matronymic formula unusual for a male ruler. Scholars are divided on whether Abiel was a reigning queen, a dynastic founder-figure, or simply a house name.
nodes.src: Potts (1991; 2002) reviews the readings
